198) And yet, as we will see, this process is not infinite—for only a finite entity is dialectical.

A moment arrives when the final synthesis coincides with the first thesis. This shows that the entity’s becoming has been completed, and therefore that its dialectical, meaning historical, existence has also come to an end.
But we will discuss this later.
199) In general, the “dialectical” order corresponds to the order of time—that is, to chronological order.
But the antithesis often begins to appear before the thesis has been fully developed, and so on.
This can make the dialectical order seem “abstract,” as though it did not correspond to the real temporal process.
200) Sometimes the antithesis takes the form of complete annihilation—for example, “suicide.”

In such a case we must show why this happens, in what sense it represents, so to speak, a “mistake” made by the entity, and finally in what the “abstract” or “non-dialectical” character of this self-negation consists.
201) In a certain sense, even the synthesis is only an abstraction.
What really exists is the entire dialectical sequence.
To isolate the synthesis or any single nature is therefore just as “abstract” as isolating the thesis or the antithesis.
But as long as history has not ended, the philosopher is forced to stop at whatever stage has so far been reached.
That stage may be synthetic, but it may equally well be thetic or antithetic.
One might say that the philosopher has a real “chance of success” only if he lives during a synthetic age.

Even then, if that age does not bring history to an end, his philosophy will inevitably remain incomplete somewhere. It will remain “abstract” and, a fortiori, unfinished, which means that it will not be absolutely true.
It will be a philosophy, not sophia or wisdom.

202) As we will soon see, the difference between historical time and natural time finds its formal, ontological expression in the fact that the future dominates historical time, whereas either the past or the present dominates natural time.
The present dominates in inorganic nature.
The past dominates in living nature.
203) This “slogan” has the character of simple “banditry” only when an isolated individual uses it for his personal benefit.
If an entire oppressed social class adopts the same slogan, it becomes, by that very fact, purely revolutionary.
204) Strictly speaking, as we will now see, all that follows necessarily from human finitude is that human beings do not depend on “God”—or that there is no interaction between humanity and God.
More precisely, “God” does not act upon human beings.
The most formal definition of the divine is, in general, something that can act upon human beings while human beings cannot act upon it.
For example, as long as the planets were thought to act upon human beings without any reciprocal action, they were regarded as “divine.”
Once Newton showed us that in the natural world every action has an equal reaction, the natural world as a whole ceased to appear “divine.”
Starting from human finitude alone, we can still admit that somewhere outside the world there may exist some sort of “God” about whom we know nothing.
But God and humanity could have no relation to one another.

Epicurus, for example, accepted a “God” or “gods” of this kind. He was also someone who correctly affirmed and emphasized human finitude, and on that basis denied any interaction between “God” and human beings.
But people with a religious temperament have always understood very clearly that such “theism” is in practice atheism.
The only “God” that interests us is one capable of affecting us.
A divinity that takes no interest whatever in us does not exist for us.
This “anthropological” or “moral” atheism therefore follows necessarily from the finitude of human existence.
205) There are so many different “gods” that it is difficult to find a definition common to all of them.
But all undoubtedly share the character of being “beyond” the world—of transcendence.
And conversely, the more “transcendent” a divinity is, the more “divine” it is.
Rudolf Otto, in Das Heilige, described this “beyond” well as the “wholly other” in relation to the world.
206) Of course, we can know what dialectic is only on the basis of these claims about human beings.

207) All references to Hegel’s Phenomenology are to the edition prepared by Johannes Hoffmeister in 1937: Hegel, Sämtliche Werke, vol. II, Leipzig, F. Meiner, 1937. This was F. Meiner’s fourth edition of the Phenomenology.
208) Spinoza adds that if the falling stone could speak, it would claim that it was falling “freely.”
But he forgets that the stone does not speak.
And he never explains why human beings speak whereas stones do not.
Human beings possess self-consciousness and therefore speech only because they are free—that is, antithetical—whereas the stone is not.
By denying human freedom, Spinoza is therefore unable, from within his own position, to explain one of the fundamental qualities of humanity: reason or discourse, logos.
Spinoza failed to recognize negativity in human beings, and this is the fundamental defect of his philosophy.
His criticism of the traditional understanding of freedom as freedom of choice, however, is entirely correct.
209) As we will see, this does not mean that one should always negate everything and everyone.

That is the mistake made by all kinds of “anarchists,” “nihilists,” and “Trotskyists.” They want to stop the dialectic at the antithesis, forgetting that the antithesis does not exist without and outside a synthesis.
Such “ultra-revolutionary” behaviour always leads to disaster, because a “pure” antithesis—that is, pure negativity—is equivalent to nothingness.
What one must, and can, negate is a thesis: a historical actuality that is already “dead,” an already “old” regime.
But as long as an actuality is still alive—meaning that it is still “making” or “creating” itself, and therefore remains revolutionary—it must be actively affirmed.
To negate it is merely to return to the thesis, which means counter-revolution.
That our Soviet actuality is still revolutionary in precisely this sense—that it remains in a period of creative “becoming”—is obvious to everyone, or at least ought to be.
210) Hegel plays on the word Erinnerung, “memory” or “recollection,” which can also be read, if one wishes, as Er-innerung: “internalization” or “bringing inward.”
211) In a certain sense, the whole of the Phenomenology is nothing other than a “recollection”—Erinnerung and Er-innerung.
By knowing history in its phenomenological aspect, the author takes it into himself, absorbs it into his consciousness, and thereby makes that consciousness “total,” meaning capable of omniscience.
212) In this sense, one could say, for example, that Nicholas II—or Louis XVI—was thetic; Lenin—or Robespierre—was antithetic; while Stalin—or Napoleon—is synthetic.
213) Bourgeois and “vulgar” materialism says, in Büchner’s words, that “a human being is what he eats.”
Hegel, and after him Marx, instead proclaim, in accordance with their conception, that a human being is what he does.
Here “does” must be understood in the strong sense: what a human being creates through work and struggle by negating what already exists.
214) Mathematically, this is explained by the fact that all “laws of nature” are “analytic functions.”
At least, that is the position of classical physics.
It can be shown that the “statistical indeterminism” of quantum mechanics changes nothing essential here.
But this would take us too far.
215) Biology has, in any case, so far always dealt with continuous phenomena rather than with their “differential rupture.”
And even if we assume that physics can completely explain life, a cat will still remain a cat despite the physical explanation.
When we speak of a cat as a cat, rather than as a complex of electrons and so on, we are speaking of something that occupies a certain interval of time.
That means the cat necessarily includes a past. It has to be studied “from birth to death.”
216) The egg’s outward appearance—that is, its “present”—will not help us here. Nor will its biological or chemical analysis.
We know that an egg with this biochemical structure came from a hen only because we already know that eggs of this kind are laid only by hens.
In other words, we understand both the present and the future from the past, and only from the past.
217) There were, of course, real or “material” causes—above all economic ones—that brought the Empire into existence.
But we are not now discussing the real or objective causes of historical events.
We are discussing why a particular event is regarded as historical.
If one prefers, I am speaking about the historical phenomenon, not the historical fact.
I want to show why the “Rubicon” made such an extraordinary impression on people that they remembered this particular night and still speak today of “crossing the Rubicon.”
Whether Caesar’s night at the Rubicon was itself genuinely “historical” or partly legendary makes no difference to me here.
218) The time in which “dreams,” “utopias,” and similar things exist is characterized by the future falling directly into the present without passing through the past.
In other words, it ignores the given circumstances inherited from the past.
In the dialectical time of real historical action, by contrast, the future enters the present through the past, as we will now see.
The past therefore serves as an intermediary between future and present.
The present is thus “mediated,” and for that reason dialectical or historical—that is, human in the strong sense of the word.
219) It is not only the proletarian who sacrifices private interests for the interests of his class and his class state.
The bourgeois does the same thing: he pays taxes, takes part in wars, and spends money on propaganda.
The difference is that, within the bourgeois class, private interests are treated as ends in themselves, so long as they do not conflict with the interests of the class as a whole.
The proletarian, by contrast, ultimately sacrifices even his proletarian interests in order to establish a classless society.

220) Bourgeois thinkers love to chatter about “individuality” and “personality.” And because they neither know nor understand Marxism, they very often even try to set their “individualism” against Marx’s doctrine. Yet they fail to understand what Hegel and Marx had already understood: as long as classes and nation-states exist, the “person” will always be degraded, and “individuality” will remain little more than the empty talk of “individualists.” It is therefore absurd to be an “individualist” without also being a Marxist—that is, without striving for a worldwide socialist revolution that will “liberate” individuals by destroying classes and the social barriers between them.
